entries.title: DR Congo reports over 10,000 Ebola cases as the outbreak spreads abroad, with no approved vaccine or specific treatment for the Bundibugyo virus
entries.summary: DR Congo has reported more than 10,000 Ebola cases and nearly 4,900 deaths. The outbreak involves a virus for which there is no approved vaccine or specific treatment, complicating efforts to contain its spread.
entries.content:
October 27, 2026

DR Congo has reported more than 10,000 Ebola cases and nearly 4,900 deaths. The outbreak involves a virus for which there is no approved vaccine or specific treatment, complicating efforts to contain its spread.

Health authorities in the Democratic Republic of Congo reported that Ebola cases had risen to 10,060, with 4,887 deaths since the outbreak was identified in mid-May.

The outbreak involves the Bundibugyo virus, for which there is no approved vaccine or specific treatment. The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention has described it as the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history.

Where else have cases been reported?

Kenya has confirmed nine infections, including two deaths, after a patient traveled from DR Congo through Uganda to the capital, Nairobi.

Nigeria also confirmed an infection in a Swiss woman, the wife of a Swiss diplomat, who fell ill after visiting Uganda. Authorities are investigating where she contracted the virus. She was evacuated to Switzerland.

Why is the outbreak difficult to contain?

Ebola spreads through direct contact with the blood or other bodily fluids of an infected person. It can cause fever, diarrhea and, in some cases, bleeding.

Early symptoms can resemble malaria, potentially delaying isolation and treatment.

The lack of an approved vaccine or specific treatment against the Bundibugyo virus further complicates efforts to control the outbreak.

If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your preferred Source on Google, so you'll always see our verified news first.

Edited by: Wesley Rahn

entries.title: Germany's Merz says erosion of global order means middle powers in Europe and Asia must be more assertive
entries.summary: During a visit to Singapore, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said Europe and Germany want to increase free trade with open competition, reliability and a rules-based order.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany news: Merz in Asia says middle powers must 'assert ' interests

Published October 27, 2026last updated October 27, 2026

During a visit to Singapore, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said Europe and Germany want to increase free trade with open competition, reliability and a rules-based order.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • German Chancellor Merz is on a multi-day tour of Asia to promote new forms of cooperation and trade
  • Germany's defense minister calls for 'a stronger Europe within a stronger NATO'
  • Court to decide whether to proceed with case against Nord Stream sabotage suspect

Keep reading for a roundup of what's making news in Germany on Tuesday, October 27, 2026:

Don't want to miss our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google.

Skip next section NSU terrorist Beate Zschäpe to stay in prison until at least 2035

NSU terrorist Beate Zschäpe to stay in prison until at least 2035

Convicted right-wing terrorist Beate Zschäpe's request for early release from prison was denied with a court ruling that she would remain behind bars for at least nine more years.

Munich's Higher Regional Court on Tuesday set her minimum term at at least 24 years and refused to suspend the sentence to probation. By determining her guilt to be particularly severe, the court effectively ruled out her release after 15 years, which, including her time in pretrial detention, would have expired this year.

The Munich court said Zschäpe, currently 51, still had a good chance of leaving prison alive.

The decision is not yet legally binding, and the defense and the Federal Prosecutor's Office can appeal.

Zschäpe had been sentenced to life in prison in 2018 as an accomplice in the National Socialist Underground (NSU) murders that killed 10 people, mainly individuals with an immigrant background as well as a police officer.

The terror group went undetected for a decade. Zschäpe's fellow NSU members, Uwe Mundlos and Uwe Böhnhardt, injured several people with bomb attacks in Cologne and killed themselves to avoid arrest in 2011.

Under normal conditions, a convict who receives a life sentence in Germany can apply for parole after 15 years.

Skip next section IN DEPTH: Harry Kane breaks Bayern and Bundesliga's Ballon d'Or drought

IN DEPTH: Harry Kane breaks Bayern and Bundesliga's Ballon d'Or drought

Bayern Munich striker Harry Kane has won football's most prestigious individual prize, beating Kylian Mbappe and Lamine Yamal. Kane has developed even more in the Bundesliga despite an uneven league.

Skip next section Pistorius wants 'stronger Europe within a stronger NATO'

Pistorius wants 'stronger Europe within a stronger NATO'

German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius, along with his counterparts from France, Italy, Poland and the UK, authored an op-ed calling Russia "the most acute and long-term threat to Euro-Atlantic security and stability."

In the article, published online and in Tuesday's Tagesspiegel newspaper, the defense ministers wrote they "share a deep conviction" that European countries need to do more to ensure their own security and aim to build "a stronger Europe within a stronger NATO."

The ministers, however, added that the United States would remain an "indispensable ally."

The pronouncement comes as many in Europe are wary of US President Donald Trump's commitment to the NATO military alliance.

The US leader has threatened to leave the group and to seize control of Greenland, a territory of fellow NATO member Denmark. US presidents have repeatedly called for European NATO members to contribute more to the alliance's military capabilities.

As US support for Ukraine also appears to waver, the five defense ministers reiterated their political, military and financial support for Kyiv as it fights of Russia's full-scale invasion.

Skip next section Merz: Collapse of global order threatens middle powers in Europe and Asia

Merz: Collapse of global order threatens middle powers in Europe and Asia

In Singapore, to start a four-day business-oriented trip that will also bring him to Japan and South Korea, Chancellor Friedrich Merz said it was up to European and Asian nations to find their spot amid a changing global order.

"We must assert our interests in an international environment shaped by renewed great-power rivalry," Merz said.

With a view to unpredictable tariffs imposed by the United States under President Donald Trump and trade restrictions from China, Merz emphasized the stability offered by Germany and the rest of Europe.

"This is a deliberate counterpoint to what we are currently seeing. We want to do things differently, and we want to show that there is a better way," Merz said, adding that Europe sought to expand partnerships to increase free trade with open competition, reliability and a rules-based order.

He also called for increased international investment and cooperation.

"Under the federal government I lead, investment opportunities will be continuously improved," Merz said following a meeting with Singapore Prime Minister Lawrence Wong. "I encounter a great deal of confidence here in Germany and in Europe as locations for investment."

The German leader called for a new free-trade agreement between the 27-member European Union and the Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP), comprising 12 countries across five continents, including Australia, Canada, Japan, Mexico and the United Kingdom. Neither the United States nor China is part of the CPTPP.

For his part, Wong said investment in Germany and Europe would continue.

"Many of our investors, including our sovereign wealth funds, have been investing in Germany for a long time," Wong said. "They will continue to invest because they are confident that, in the long term, Germany and Europe have potential."

Merz and Wong agreed their nations would work to expand cooperation in security and defense as well as trade, investment, sustainable energy and artificial intelligence.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Guten Morgen and welcome to our daily coverage of what's making news in Germany. 

While we follow the news here in Berlin and Bonn, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz is in Singapore, speaking about international cooperation among middle-power countries in Europe and Asia amid a "renewed great-power rivalry."

Today, we're also expecting a decision on whether to proceed with a case against a Nord Stream sabotage suspect and a report on Germany's ongoing search for a nuclear waste storage facility.

Not to mention a car ramming last night near the northern German city of Hannover that has left several people with serious injuries, while the suspects are still on the run.

entries.title: Two men face UK national security charges following an incident near RAF Fairford, with police suspecting Iranian state involvement
entries.summary: British prosecutors have charged two men over an incident near RAF Fairford in September. Police suspect Iranian involvement in the case at a base used for US strikes on Iran.
entries.content:
October 27, 2026

British prosecutors have charged two men over an incident near RAF Fairford in September. Police suspect Iranian involvement in the case at a base used for US strikes on Iran.

British prosecutors said Tuesday that two men had been charged under the National Security Act in connection with a September incident near RAF Fairford, an airbase used by US forces to launch strikes on Iran.

US bombers were withdrawn from Fairford on security grounds shortly after the arrests immediately after the incident.

What have police said about the Fairford suspects?

The Crown Prosecution Service charged Mohmed A., 24, of London, with engaging in conduct likely to materially assist a foreign intelligence service. Counterterrorism police chief Laurence Taylor said investigators believed the country involved was Iran.

Nouman E., 24, also of London, was charged with entering a prohibited place for a purpose prejudicial to the UK on August 22. Both men were due to appear in court later Tuesday.

Nouman E. was initially arrested near the Gloucestershire base on September 27 and rearrested on October 20.

A separate suspect, a 25-year-old British-Iranian dual national also arrested on October 20, was released without charge over the suspected intelligence offense. He remains on bail following an October 1 arrest on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts. Five other men also remain on police bail.

How did the Fairford investigation begin?

Armed police responded to reports of three suspicious vehicles near the base on September 27 and arrested five men. Scores of residents were evacuated as police and military bomb-disposal experts searched the area for explosives.

Police have said they consider Iranian state involvement "highly likely."

"We have seen a range of incidents in recent months that we believe have been directed by the Iranian state," said Laurence Taylor, head of UK counterterrorism policing.

He said police were working with MI5, Britain's domestic intelligence service, to counter the threat and urged the public to report concerns.

Iran has denied involvement, although it has previously said it considers bases used to attack its territory legitimate targets.

Edited by: Wesley Rahn

entries.title: Police in northern Germany search for suspects after car ramming overnight injures several
entries.summary: A person intentionally drove into a group of people in a northern German town, police have said. Three people have been taken into custody in what police said was likely a gang confrontation.
entries.content:
October 27, 2026

A person intentionally drove into a group of people in a northern German town, police have said. Three people have been taken into custody in what police said was likely a gang confrontation.

A BMW was driven ​deliberately ‌into a group of people, leaving ‌four to five of ‌them ​with some serious but not life-threatening injuries in Neustadt am Rübenberge late on Monday night, police said on Tuesday morning.

A police patrol making routine traffic checks in town near Hannover in the state of Lower Saxony, intervened, shooting at the car to stop it.

"The officers witnessed the incident as it happened and opened fire on the vehicle after it had been driven into the group of people," the spokesperson said.

Organized crime suspected

Police announced that they had taken three people into custody at the BMW owner's address.

A police spokesperson added that initial findings indicated the ramming was an act of gang violence between organized crime families, that the individuals involved knew each other and that the perpetrators likely targeted the group of people and were not acting at random.

Several suspects had fled the scene of the ramming on foot, police had said.

"The sequence of events and the exact roles of those involved are still under investigation," the spokesperson said, adding that forensic analysis of the cars and ramming scene was ongoing.

A reporter for the German DPA news agency described several damaged cars, with flat tires, a smashed rear window and bullet holes.

Edited by: Wesley Rahn

entries.title: India news: Arunachal sees fresh violence over proposed dam
entries.summary: More violence erupted in India's northeastern state of Arunachal Pradesh over proposed hydroelectric projects that locals are protesting. Also, India's top court will hear pleas against the poll body chief. More on DW.
entries.content:
India

India news: Arunachal sees more violence as anti-dam protests spread

Published October 27, 2026last updated October 27, 2026

More violence erupted in India's northeastern state of Arunachal Pradesh over proposed hydroelectric projects that locals are protesting. Also, India's top court will hear pleas against the poll body chief. More on DW.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Protests and violence spread in Arunachal Pradesh over proposed Menga Dam
  • Supreme Court to hear petitions against election body chief Gyanesh Kumar voter roll revision

Here are the top headlines from India on Tuesday, October 27:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section India's east coast braces as cyclone 'Arnab' approaches

India's east coast braces as cyclone 'Arnab' approaches

The Indian coastal states of Odisha, Andhra Pradesh, took a number of steps including shutting schools, issuing helpline numbers and moving vulnerable people to safety as the severe cyclonic storm "Arnab" approaches.

The Indian Meteorological Department (IMD) on Tuesday forecast isolated by "extremely heavy rainfall" over coastal Andhra Pradesh and Odisha for Tuesday and Wednesday, adding that nearby Chhattisgarh would experience similar conditions on Wednesday.

Much of the rest of India, including Delhi, will also see moderate weather impacts of winds and rainfall due to the cyclone, the press statement said.

Other eastern states including West Bengal and Jharkhand will also see heavy rainfall over the next three days, it added.

The cyclone which formed over the Bay of Bengal on Monday morning is expected to make landfall in Andhra Pradesh on Wednesday.

Odisha shut schools and banned fishing and is preparing to evacuate nearly 50,000 people to safer places to prepare for the storm, local media reported.

Andhra Pradesh also implemented similar measures to ensure "zero loss of life and minimal damage to infrastructure."

Train services were also impacted with India's South Coast Railway suspending 53 train services over October 27 and 28 due to the storm.

India's biggest air carriers IndiGo and Air India said flights to and from Andhra Pradesh's capital city of Vishakhapatnam would be impacted on October 27 due to weather conditions brought by the storm.

They advised travelers to check their flight status and book book alternate flights in cases of cancellations.

Skip next section Election body defends SIR roll-out in top court ahead of hearing

Election body defends SIR roll-out in top court ahead of hearing

The Election Commission of India (ECI) on Monday defended its decision to carry out the "Special Intensive Revision (SIR)" of electoral rolls, saying the exercise was undertaken legally and approved unanimously, the Press Trust of India news agency reported.

The defense was made in a counter affidavit filed in the Supreme Court of India ahead of today's hearing on petitions against poll-body chief Gyanesh Kumar.

In September, The Indian Express newspaper published a major investigative report citing irregularities in the voter revision exercise while alleging an internal rift.

The report said Chief Election Commissioner Kumar reportedly made unilateral decisions without informing the other two election commissioners as required under law.

The report led to nationwide protests led by student unions and India's Cockroach movement who argue that Kumar took biased decisions to the benefit of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government, eroding the people's vote in the world's largest democracy.

The protests were met with a massive police response  and detentions. 

India's opposition parties are also conducting a unified campaign against Kumar and Modi, calling for the former's removal from power and a rollback of voter names deleted under SIR.

India's largest opposition party Indian National Congress (INC), along with its regional allies, is planning a 'Save the Vote' march in Delhi in November. It has called for Indian masses including students, workers and farmers to join in. 

Skip next section Arunachal calls in police reinforcements amid protests

Arunachal calls in police reinforcements amid protests

Authorities in Arunachal Pradesh called in reinforcements to the town of Pasighat in anticipation of more protests over a hydroelectric dam.

News outlet NDTV reported that the state police called in dozens of Rapid Action Forces (RAF), a special federal police unit.

More companies of Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF) were rushed in from Assam to the Siang Valley Region, the report said, adding that a total of About 34 companies of Central Armed Police Force (CAPF) was deployed in the region.

Regional newspaper Arunachal Times reported that about 30 companies of CAPF, alongside state and paramilitary forces were in the region to manage the tense protests.

The force reallocation comes days after protests against Siang Upper Multipurpose Project (SUMP) turned violent in Pasighat on October 23. Mobs reportedly vandalized lawmakers' houses and set local offices on fire.

Skip next section Anti-dam protests spread in Arunachal Pradesh

Anti-dam protests spread in Arunachal Pradesh

Violent protests broke out against a proposed hydroelectric project in Arunachal Pradesh on Monday in Daporijo town.

Normal life in Daporijo was interrupted as student organizations implemented a 12-hour general strike over the 1,605-megawatt Upper Subansiri hydroelectric plant, also known as the Menga Dam project.

The protesters are demanding authorities permanently withdraw the power project.

Anti-damn protests have been building up in the northeastern mountain state,  with locals fearing mass displacement, loss of ancestral land, ecological losses and seismic risks.

News outlets reported that tensions escalated during the strike leading to fresh violence. At least one police vehicle was damaged and a police constable injured, the Arunachal Times reported. The report said that supporters of the strike also allegedly vandalized an office rented by India's flagship hydroelectric power generation company, setting office equipment on fire.

The Times of India also reported that local police conducted a flag march and appealed for peace.

In the village of Taliha, residents voice strong opposition to the Menga Damn project and the related land assessment exercise in motion. Protesters blocked a bridge to restrict movement, Arunachal Times reported, adding that their demonstrations were largely peaceful.

Not the only controversial dam

Protests and related violence shook Pasighat on October 23 after police fired tear gas at youths protesting the proposed 11,000-megawatt Siang Upper Multipurpose Project (SUMP). That's a different, larger but an equally as controversial project as the Menga Dam.

Protesters had allegedly set fire to buildings and vehicles then as well, prompting police forces to arrest dozens of demonstrators.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Hello and welcome to DW's India news blog.

This is Mahima Kapoor reporting from Studio Delhi and I will be your guide through what's making headlines across the nation.

The state of Arunachal Pradesh saw fresh violence as locals there protest a proposed hydroelectric project.

This comes days after violent protests broke out in in a different part of the state over a different but equally controversial hydroelectric project.

Meanwhile in Delhi, India's top court is set to hear petitions against India's Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over reported irregularities and decisions concerning the controversial revision of electoral rolls.

Before the hearing, the poll body defended itself in an affidavit, saying all decisions were taken unanimously.

Stay tuned for all of this and more.

entries.title: Israel election: Israelis vote for 1st time since October 7 terror attack
entries.summary: Israel's longest-serving prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, faces a battle to stay in power amid fierce competition from a bloc led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot. Arab parties are projected to play kingmakers.
entries.content:
Israel

Israel election: Israelis vote for 1st time since October 7 attack

Published October 27, 2026last updated October 27, 2026

Israel's longest-serving prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, faces a battle to stay in power amid fierce competition from a bloc led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot. Arab parties are projected to play kingmakers.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Israelis voting to elect Knesset
  • Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving prime minister, faces a staunch challenge to his grip on power
  • His chief rival is former military chief Gadi Eisenkot
  • Eisenkot's Yashar party has polled higher than Netanyahu's Likud party
  • Arab parties are projected to play kingmaker in post-election coalition talks
  • This is the first election since the 2023 October 7 Hamas-led terror attack and the subsequent two-year Gaza war

Follow below for all the latest on the Israeli election on October 27, 2026, and its aftermath:

Skip next section Early Israel election turnout highest in decades

Early Israel election turnout highest in decades

Voter turnout in the first three hours of the Israeli general election was the highest in decades, Israel's Central Elections Committee said on Tuesday.

According to the committee, nationwide turnout by mid-morning was already at 16.68%, the highest at this stage of the vote since 1981 and up from 15.9% at the same time in the 2022 election.

"By 10 a.m., more than 1,200,000 Israelis had voted," said the committee's acting director general, Dean Livne.

Total voter turnout in Israeli general elections approached 80% the 1990s but hasn't been higher than 72.3% since the turn of the century. Turnout at the last general election in 2022 was 70.6%.

Turnout among Arab Israelis is expected to be particularly important given the role Arab parties could play as potential kingmakers in coalition talks.

"Our vote will change the government," predicted Mansour Abbas, head of the Islamist Ra'am party as he cast his vote, adding that he hoped turnout would surpass 70% in Arab communities.

Arabs in Israel make up about 18% of the electorate, and pre-election surveys have suggested a sharp increase in voter participation.

Data from the Midgam Research Institute cited by the Qatar-owned The New Arab indicates that turnout within the Arab community could rise to between 62% and 63%, up from approximately 53% in previous elections. The National, based in the United Arab Emirates, said its sources were predicting an "astronomical" Arab turnout.

Skip next section How does Israel's election work?

How does Israel's election work?

Who is eligible to vote?

Around 7.3 million Israelis (including around 1.2 million Palestinian citizens of Israel) are eligible to vote on Tuesday.

More than 640,000 young Israelis will be eligible to vote in a general election for the first time.

Around 3.1 million Palestinians living under Israeli occupation in the West Bank do not have the right to vote in Israeli elections, but 500,000 illegal settlers in those territories do.

A further 350,000 Palestinians live in Israeli-occupied East Jerusalem and also cannot vote, whereas around 230,000 Israelis living there can.

The US-based non-profit America-Israel Democracy Coalition (AID Coalition) has organized a "Fly&Vote" initiative, with as many as 67,000 voters returning to Israel to participate in the election, based on surveys of expatriates and registration data.

The coalition said half are coming from the US, with others from Europe, Canada, Australia and New Zealand. Israel does not have postal voting.

How does the voting system work?

Israel is a parliamentary democracy and voters elect a legislature rather than choosing their prime minister directly. Voters choose a party "list."

Israel uses a proportional representation system under which 120 parliamentary seats are distributed roughly in proportion to a party's share of the vote.

To enter parliament (known as the Knesset), parties must receive at least 3.25% of valid votes, which is equivalent to roughly four seats.

The party which can command a majority of at least 61 seats is called upon to form a government. No single party has ever won an outright majority, so Israel has always been governed by coalitions. Polls suggest this year will be no different.

Unlike many other democracies around the world, Israel is not divided up into geographic electoral districts.

Rather than electing individual lawmakers to represent local areas, voters in Tel Aviv, Jerusalem and Haifa all choose from the same party lists in one, single, nationwide constituency.

When polling stations close at 10 p.m. local time (9 p.m. CET), broadcasters will publish their first exit polls, offering an initial indication of the results. Official results are scheduled to be published on November 4.

Skip next section Arab-Israeli parties: Potential kingmakers in Israel's future ruling coalition?

Arab-Israeli parties: Potential kingmakers in Israel's future ruling coalition?

While the main competition for the largest number of seats is between Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud and Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar, the Arab parties are projected to play a key role in determining Israel's next ruling coalition.

For a party or coalition to rule, it needs to secure 61 seats in the Knesset.

As per a recent Channel 12 poll, Eisenkot's bloc is hovering around 55 seats, while Netanyahu's bloc is trailing behind with some 51 seats. This means that either bloc would need to form coalitions in order to rule, should the election results come out similar to the polls.

The most likely parties to tip the scales are the Joint List (projected to win around 9 seats) and the Ra'am (projected to win around 5 seats). The Arab minority, who are Palestinian by heritage but Israeli by nationality, make up around a fifth of Israel's eligible voters. Polls suggest a higher turnout rate for the Arab voters than seen in previous elections.

Netanyahu's Likud and Ben-Gvir's Otzma Yehudi parties attempted last month to ban the Joint List and Ra'am from running in the race, but Israel's Supreme Court reversed the parties' disqualification earlier in October.

Both Eisenkot and Netanyahu have ruled out an alliance with the Arab parties. But analysts suggest such stances are not set in stone and can shift amid coalition talks, a move Netanyahu himself has resorted to in the past.

Skip next section Gadi Eisenkot: Who is Netanyahu's main opponent?

Gadi Eisenkot: Who is Netanyahu's main opponent?

The Israeli general election is considered by many to be a verdict on the country's longest-serving prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu.

But who is the opposition, and what do they stand for?

The main opposition force is a so-called "change bloc," a mixed group of center-right and some left-wing parties led by the newly formed Yashar (honesty) party and its leader Gadi Eisenkot.

A relative political newcomer, Eisenkot is the son of Moroccan immigrants who rose to become the chief of the staff of the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) between 2015 and 2019.

Eisenkot has positioned himself squarely in opposition to Netanyahu in terms of his personality — an unpolished man of the people in contrast to the highly stylized and controlling prime minister.

Campaigning on accountability, political reform, and national unity, Eisenkot has sharply criticized Netanyahu's leadership before and after the October 7 Hamas attacks.

But his politics don't differ massively and, although he has emphasized equal rights for all Israeli citizens, he has been ambiguous on the idea of a two-state solution since October 7.

While backing Israel's military operations, he argues the government lacks a clear strategy and has called for an independent inquiry into the failures surrounding the attacks. His military record and the death of his son in the Gaza war have strengthened his standing among many voters

The parties in Eisenkot's bloc all have ideological differences but are united by their goal of removing Netanyahu from power.

Skip next section Polls open in Israel election

Polls open in Israel election

Voting began in Israel at 7 a.m. local time (6 a.m. CET) on Tuesday in the first general election since the deadly Hamas attack on October 7, 2023, and the devastating war in Gaza unleashed by Israel in response.

Some 7.3 million Israeli citizens are eligible to vote, with polls showing a bloc led by right-wing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the country's longest-serving premier, neck and neck with Gadi Eisenkot's centrist opposition alliance.

Most polling stations will close at 10 p.m. local time (8 p.m. UTC).

Skip next section WATCH: Netanyahu's final campaign? — Israel heads to the polls

WATCH: Netanyahu's final campaign? — Israel heads to the polls

There's a lot at stake in this election: The fallout and questions of political accountability for the attacks of October 7, 2023; mandatory military service for ultra-Orthodox men and sharing the burden of national defense; along with Israel's standing in the international community.

Nowhere can the division within Israeli society be more felt than in debate over Benjamin Netanyahu.

For the past four years, Israel's long-standing prime minister has led what has been described as the most right-wing government in the country's history. He broke with political convention by forming an alliance with ultranationalist politician Itamar Ben-Gvir.

Many Israelis want to see an end to this government. They blame it for the failures surrounding Hamas' terror attack and for the country's growing isolation internationally. Many are placing their hopes in Gadi Eisenkot, who has emerged as a leading opposition figure to challenge Netanyahu.

Skip next section Security fears and domestic divides define Israel's election battle

Security fears and domestic divides define Israel's election battle

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his top challenger Gadi Eisenkot are both against the creation of an independent Palestinian state, meaning the election is not expected to lead to major policy changes that could revive the long-stalled peace process.

Here are some of the other major campaign issues:

  • Security and the War: Voters are focused on the management of the Israel-Hamas war, the future of Gaza, and handling threats from Iran and Hezbollah.
  • Military Service: There is an intense debate over whether the exemption for ultra-Orthodox (Haredi) men should be extended or whether they should be required to serve in the military like other Jewish citizens.
  • The Justice System: There are deep disagreements over proposed judicial reforms that would change the balance of power between elected politicians and the Supreme Court.
  • The Economy: Voters are highly concerned about the cost of living, housing prices, inflation, and war-related spending, although these are not the primary campaign issues.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Israelis head to the polls today to elect a new Knesset in what is expected to be a tightly contested race.

Incumbent Benjamin Netanyahu, the country's longest-serving prime minister, is fighting to stay in power, with several court cases awaiting him if he loses office.

Polls suggest his opponent, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, is in the lead.

Stay tuned as we closely follow the election, its results and the wider implications for the region.

entries.title: Brazil elections: Merz, world leaders congratulate Lula on his win
entries.summary: Brazilian President Lula secured a surprise win over far-right challenger Flavio Bolsonaro, whose party recognizes Lula's election victory.
entries.content:
Brazil

Brazil elections: Merz, world leaders congratulate Lula on his win

Published October 25, 2026last updated October 27, 2026

Brazilian President Lula secured a surprise win over far-right challenger Flavio Bolsonaro, whose party recognizes Lula's election victory.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Left-wing incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva defeated Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of the far-right former President Jair Bolsonaro

  • It was a tight runoff, with Lula winning 51.7% of the vote against Bolsonaro’s 48.2%, official results showed

  • In his victory speech, Lula urged more regulation of big tech platforms after allegations that Meta interfered in the race

  • Bolsonaro refused to concede, but his party recognizes Lula's victory

  • Trading was suspended on the stock market for half an hour on Monday morning as shares and Brazil's real currency tumbled

  • Several Latin American leaders congratulated Lula on win

  • Germany's Merz said he looks forward to 'deepening strategic ties' with Brazil

  • US President Trump said the vote 'looked terrible,' but added, 'I like Lula'

This blog is now closed.

Keep reading for developments from the second round of Brazil's presidential election on Sunday, October 25, with continued coverage into Monday, October 26.

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section Thank you for reading

Thank you for reading

Thank you or obrigado for following our live news blog coverage of the Brazilian presidential election runoff.

We're sure to have more coverage of Brazilian politics, Lula and Flavio Bolsonaro in the coming days and weeks.

Stay tuned for more with DW.

Skip next section Bolsonaro's party recognizes Lula's election victory

Bolsonaro's party recognizes Lula's election victory

Brazil's Liberal Party has acknowledged President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva's election victory, breaking with its own candidate Flavio Bolsonaro, who has refused to concede defeat.

"We recognize the presidential election results," party leader Valdemar Costa Neto said in a statement on Monday. "But we believe the issues raised need to be properly clarified."

The statement marks a clear break with Bolsonaro's position. The senator has vowed to seek the annulment of Sunday's runoff result, claiming that a two-hour extension of voting favored Lula.

The extension was ordered due to transport problems in several cities that made it difficult for voters to reach polling stations. Bolsonaro's own campaign had also requested more voting time in some regions because of heavy rainfall.

According to electoral officials, the extension did not change the outcome of the election.

Bolsonaro has yet to publicly respond to his party's statement.

Skip next section Flavio Bolsonaro says he is banned from leaving Brazil after election defeat

Flavio Bolsonaro says he is banned from leaving Brazil after election defeat

Defeated Brazilian presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro says he has been ordered to surrender his passports and is banned from leaving the country.

The right-wing senator said federal police approached him after he visited his imprisoned father, former President Jair Bolsonaro.

"I was ordered right on the street to hand over my passports, and I'm also prohibited from leaving the country," Bolsonaro said in a video posted on social media.

He called the move "a clear attempt to intimidate me" and claimed the order came from Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes. Neither the court nor federal police immediately confirmed the reported ruling.

Bolsonaro said the decision was based on comments by his brother Eduardo, who had suggested he should leave Brazil if he lost the election. He denied having any plans to flee the country and said he would comply with the order.

Skip next section Trump says Brazil vote 'looked terrible to me' but adds, 'I like Lula'

Trump says Brazil vote 'looked terrible to me' but adds, 'I like Lula'

Ask, and you shall receive — sometimes anyway! Now a senior US government representative has commented on Brazil's vote.

Leaving Washington for a midterm election campaign rally, President Donald Trump told reporters that it "looked terrible" to him. 

"I didn't take sides but it looked like another rigged election frankly... it looked so corrupt, so terrible," he said.

Asked by a reporter if he wanted to "do something about the election," Trump seemed to suggest he did not, albeit repeating his criticism of the mechanics of the vote.

"Well, I'm not running Brazil. I'm running the USA. I just thought that the election was, uh — I like Lula, I get along with him very well — I just think it had a very bad look, the election. The way it was tabulated, you know? The extension given was very strange."

Skip next section US yet to comment on Brazil election

US yet to comment on Brazil election

As of 3:20 p.m. in Washington D.C. (1920 GMT), the upper echelons of US government were yet to respond to the election in Brazil on Sunday.

The only October 26 State Department press releases concerned Austria's national day and Secretary of State Marco Rubio's planned trip to Georgia later in the week for a G20 Foreign Ministers' Meeting.

Rubio had not opined on his social media channels and US President Donald Trump's Truth Social account — which only tends to pick up on stories with a tape delay unless they involve Trump directly — had remained inactive since Sunday night.

Lula and his Workers' Party often had strained relations with US governments, especially Republican ones, but this has been particularly pronounced in Trump's case.

Skip next section Recap — Why is Bolsonaro crying foul after the voting extension?

Recap — Why is Bolsonaro crying foul after the voting extension?

Just joining us and wondering how Brazil's runoff vote had a considerably clearer margin of victory than predicted and yet still ended in controversy and the losing candidate refusing to concede defeat? 

Challenger Flavio Bolsonaro's objections were focused around the evening extension of voting past the planned closing time of 5 p.m. across the country.

The decisions by a Lula-appointed Supreme Court justice on Sunday followed a complaint over allegations of pro-Bolsonaro mayors being behind public transport irregularities that may have hampered people's plans to vote.

On election night, Bolsonaro then told journalists it was "impossible to recognize the election results, given the circumstances under which things unfolded."

For now it's unclear whether, as the dust settles, Bolsonaro will continue to resist the outcome and try to encourage protests in the way his now-jailed father Jair Bolsonaro did four years ago.

But two factors in particular seem to speak against the prospects of a potential Bolsonaro challenge.

Firstly, his fairly sizeable margin of defeat — losing by slightly more than 4 million votes rather than just a few thousand — makes it much more unlikely that a two-hour extension at polling stations could have even the theoretical potential of swaying the result.

And beyond that, his camp appealed for and successfully secured permission to keep polling stations open in some of Bolsonaro's southern strongholds, after torrential rains interfered with would-be voters' travel plans.

Skip next section African leaders congratulate Lula, seek to 'advance shared interests'

African leaders congratulate Lula, seek to 'advance shared interests'

Nigerian President Bola Ahmed Tinubu was one of several African leaders to congratulate Lula on Monday, saying that his renewed mandate offered an opportunity to strengthen bilateral ties. 

"As two leading nations of the Global South, we can promote economic integration and advance our shared interests in a rapidly changing global order," Tinubu said online, saying he looked forward to expanding cooperation in a raft of areas.

Tanzanian President Samia Suluhu also extended her "sincere congratulations" to Lula. 

"Tanzania values its longstanding friendship with Brazil, and looks forward to continue building on this foundation to further strengthen bilateral relations and deepen cooperation, for the mutual benefit of our two nations," Suluhu said.

Seychelles President Patrick Herminie called the runoff election result "a powerful affirmation of the trust the Brazilian people have placed in President Lula's leadership," in comments published by his office online. 

He said Lula's win was "a testament to his lifelong commitment to the dignity and well-being of ordinary men and women," saying the Seychelles shared Lula's values like "social justice, equality of opportunity, the protection of workers and the most vulnerable, and a model of development that places people at its center."

Herminie expressed a desire to deepen bilateral cooperation, particularly in tackling climate change, protecting the oceans and advancing the interests of the Global South.

Skip next section Putin congratulates Lula, praising his 'personal contribution' to bilateral ties

Putin congratulates Lula, praising his 'personal contribution' to bilateral ties

Russian President Vladimir Putin offered congratulations to Lula in a telegram published by the Kremlin on Monday. 

"It is difficult to overstate your personal contribution to strengthening the strategic partnership between Brazil and Russia," the telegram stated.

Putin, a leader of a fellow BRICS alliance member, is one of few world leaders to have worked with Lula across all of his presidential terms, starting in 2003. 

Putin also congratulated Lula on his upcoming 81st birthday, which falls on Tuesday.

The Russian president's spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters in Moscow earlier in the day that the Kremlin welcomed Lula's re-election.

Skip next section WATCH: Brazil's Lula celebrates election victory as Bolsonaro rejects results

WATCH: Brazil's Lula celebrates election victory as Bolsonaro rejects results

Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva has won a historic fourth term after defeating far-right rival Flavio Bolsonaro in a runoff election.

It's a historic political comeback for Lula who trailed in the first round.

DW reports from Rio de Janeiro.

Skip next section Sao Paulo stock exchange halts trading over sharp drop after Lula win

Sao Paulo stock exchange halts trading over sharp drop after Lula win

Trading on the Sao Paulo stock exchange, the largest in Latin America, was suspended for 30 minutes on Monday after plummeting nearly 17% in the wake of the re-election of left-wing Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, who defeated conservative Flavio Bolsonaro.

The sharp drop in the benchmark Ibovespa index triggered a 30-minute "circuit breaker" mechanism provided for "periods of sharp market decline," according to a stock exchange statement.

Meanwhile, the US dollar surged 12% against Brazil's currency, one of the real's biggest ‌daily moves on record.

Prices of raw sugar, one of Brazil's most important exports, slid nearly 5% on the collapsing exchange rate.

Prediction markets had indicated a Bolsonaro win but the right-wing senator's refusal to concede defeat and ​his pledge to challenge the election result have added to investor uncertainty.

"Important for local financial markets will be how quickly Bolsonaro accepts the result, or at least allows the constitution to run its course," Chris Turner, a strategist at ING in London, told the Reuters news agency as attention turned to Lula's choice of finance minister — a clue as to his fiscal approach.

"The key signal for markets will ⁠be the ​next Lula administration's commitment to fiscal discipline, starting with the appointment of a new finance minister in coming weeks," RBC BlueBay Asset Management's Graham ​Stock told Reuters.

Skip next section Germany's Merz wants to deepen 'the strategic partnership' with Brazil

Germany's Merz wants to deepen 'the strategic partnership' with Brazil

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has joined the chorus of world leaders  congratulating Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva on his re-election.

"I look forward to further deepening the strategic partnership between Germany and Brazil together," Merz said in a message posted on X.

Germany and Brazil held government consultations in Hannover in April of this year, at which Merz and Lula agreed to cooperate more closely on defense and raw materials, among other things.

Skip next section Brazilian markets poised for sharp drop Monday after Lula win

Brazilian markets poised for sharp drop Monday after Lula win

Brazilian markets are bracing for heavy selling on Monday, with futures of Brazil's benchmark stock index ‌Bovespa ⁠falling ⁠nearly 15% in early Monday ​trading 

On global markets, the iShares MSCI Brazil ETF, which tracks a basket of major Brazilian stocks, plunged as much as 26% in premarket trading as investors unwind bets on a right-wing victory.

Brazilian Real November futures also fell 10% in Asian trading, while US-listed shares of Brazilian stocks dropped as well, with energy giant Petrobras plunging more than 20% and banking group Itau Unibanco cratering almost 30%.

Investors had seen election loser Flavio Bolsonaro as the candidate most likely to boost markets with fiscal austerity and deregulation, while Lula has pursued policies of redistribution and state-led development, including costly welfare programs.

Skip next section Russia says it welcomes Lula's re-election

Russia says it welcomes Lula's re-election

The Kremlin said on Monday it welcomed Lula's victory and praised what it said were his efforts to cultivate Brazil-Russia ties.

"We welcome Mr. Lula's victory. He does a lot, not only for the development of bilateral relations but also for advancing processes within the framework of BRICS," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters.

He said Russia hoped for more of the same.

Lula himself has possibly put Brazil in the Kremlin's good books by not joining Western sanctions on Russia over Moscow's invasion of Ukraine and calling for a negotiated peace.

However, he has called on all nations to adhere to the principles of sovereignty and territorial integrity enshrined in the UN Charter, thus implicitly condemning Russia's aggression.

Brazil and Russia are both members of BRICS, an international cooperation group founded in 2009 along with India and China, with South Africa joining a year later, and taking all those countries' first initials to make up its name.

It has since then been expanded to include 10 member nations in all, with a number of "partner countries" also invited in 2024.

Skip next section Votes tallied in Brazil's presidential election after polls close

Votes tallied in Brazil's presidential election after polls close

Here's a DW infographic on where the results stand:

Skip next section France, China, Spain congratulate Lula on victory

France, China, Spain congratulate Lula on victory

Messages of congratulations continue to rain in from around the world following Lula's unexpected win.

China's response was measured, with Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun saying that "China has noted that Brazil's Superior Electoral Court has announced President Lula has won the second round of the Brazilian general election, and expresses its congratulations."

Guo added that Beijing was "willing to work with Brazil to continue advancing the building of a China-Brazil community with a shared future."

French President Emmanuel Macron, after expressing his congratulations, said Brazil and France should work to "strengthen our strategic partnership."

"France and Brazil have much to build together," Macron said X, adding that the two countries should nurture their friendship "in the service of a fairer world."

Spain's prime minister, Pedro Sanchez, was more effusive, casting Lula's victory as evidence that the world is experiencing a backlash to its seeming rightwards political trajectory at present.

"A great victory for Lula! What has happened in Brazil will happen in Spain. The global progressive comeback has just begun," Sanchez, who has called snap elections in November, posted on X.

entries.title: Ukraine and Russia begin Oleshky ceasefire for aid mission
entries.summary: Around 2,000 people remain stranded in the city of Oleshky, facing severe shortages of food and medicine. The Russian-occupied town has been devastated by fighting and flooding since Moscow's invasion in 2022.
entries.content:
Ukraine

Ukraine and Russia begin Oleshky ceasefire for aid mission

October 27, 2026

Around 2,000 people remain stranded in the city of Oleshky, facing severe shortages of food and medicine. The Russian-occupied town has been devastated by fighting and flooding since Moscow's invasion in 2022.

Russia and Ukraine began a localized ceasefire early Tuesday to allow humanitarian aid into the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky in southern Ukraine.

Both sides confirmed that the truce took effect at 3 a.m. local time (0100 GMT), following an agreement brokered by US first lady Melania Trump.

Russia's Defense Ministry said its forces had stopped shelling in the Kherson sector to prepare for the humanitarian operation.

Ukraine's human rights commissioner Dmytro Lubinets also confirmed that Kyiv was observing the agreement.

"As head of the Ukrainian negotiating team, I confirm that the Ukrainian side is honoring its commitments," he wrote on Facebook.

However, it could not be independently verified whether fighting had decreased.

What is the humanitarian situation in Oleshky?

Around 2,000 people, including up to 50 children, remain trapped in Oleshky, according to Ukrainian and US estimates. The town had about 24,000 residents before Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022.

The United Nations says residents face severe shortages of food and medicine. Mines and drone attacks have made it difficult for them to leave.

Former residents told news agency AFP earlier this year that people remaining in the town were starving, sometimes hunting pigeons or surviving on food grown in their gardens.

"They've forgotten what bread is. You need flour for bread, and there's not even flour left," said Olga, who was in contact with two families still in Oleshky.

Oleshky lies across the Dnipro River from the Ukrainian-controlled city of Kherson.

Russian troops captured the town during the first days of the invasion in 2022. It suffered further destruction in June 2023 when the collapse of the Kakhovka dam caused widespread flooding.

What role did Melania Trump play in the ceasefire?

The White House said last week that Melania Trump had helped secure the agreement after holding talks with civilian negotiators from Russia and Ukraine.

Her office said the first lady had also met United Nations officials who briefed her on conditions in Oleshky.

Announcing the agreement on Friday, Trump said civilian officials from both countries would visit residents to assess their needs.

Doctors, food, drinking water and medicine are expected to reach the town before evacuation corridors are opened.

"Residents who wish to evacuate will receive coordinated support and transportation to their preferred destination. I anticipate some will want to go to Russia, and some to Ukraine," Melania Trump said.

Ukraine has accused Russia of preventing residents from leaving, an allegation Moscow denies.

Neither side has provided details about who will monitor the ceasefire. Reports have also differed over its duration, with one account saying it could last through Saturday.

What happened in Kyiv after the ceasefire began?

Russian missile attacks continued elsewhere in Ukraine as the localized ceasefire began.

Explosions shook Kyiv shortly after 3 a.m. local time Tuesday, according to witnesses, while air raid alerts sounded across several regions.

Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said the attacks had damaged the Southern Bridge and associated subway infrastructure. City authorities said traffic on the bridge had been suspended.

On Monday, a Russian missile attack on Kyiv killed at least one person and injured 10 others, including students at a dormitory. Further attacks caused casualties in Kharkiv and Pavlohrad.

"It is important that the world sees that Russia is showing nothing but a desire to kill and continue waging war," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy wrote after the attacks.

Could the Oleshky ceasefire help revive Ukraine peace talks?

The limited truce in Oleshky comes ahead of another round of US-mediated peace talks between Washington, Moscow and Kyiv, expected in November.

Negotiations have been effectively frozen since the United States and Israel launched joint strikes on Iran in February.

Previous attempts to establish ceasefires have repeatedly failed amid deep mistrust between Russia and Ukraine.

More than four and a half years after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, hundreds of thousands of soldiers and civilians have been killed, while millions have been forced to flee their homes.

Edited by: Wesley Dockery

entries.title: US seeks new charges against former FBI chief James Comey
entries.summary: The Trump administration accuses the former FBI director of leaking classified information a decade ago. Comey denies wrongdoing, while his lawyers argue the case is legally invalid and comes too late.
entries.content:
October 27, 2026

The Trump administration accuses the former FBI director of leaking classified information a decade ago. Comey denies wrongdoing, while his lawyers argue the case is legally invalid and comes too late.

The US Justice Department has launched a third attempt to prosecute former FBI Director James Comey, accusing him of illegally disclosing national defense information in 2016.

Court documents unsealed on Monday reveal allegations that Comey directed a subordinate to share classified information with a journalist.

The case marks another escalation in President Donald Trump's long-running conflict with the former FBI chief, who has denied wrongdoing.

What are the latest allegations against James Comey?

The case centers on an October 2016 New York Times article about a secret US surveillance order involving internet company Yahoo.

The order reportedly required Yahoo to scan emails for messages potentially linked to a foreign terrorist organization. It had been issued by a secret intelligence court.

Prosecutors allege that Comey instructed a staff member to contact a New York Times journalist to correct inaccurate information published by news agency Reuters the previous day.

According to the Justice Department, this resulted in the illegal transfer of classified national defense information to an unauthorized person.

However, the allegations have already been investigated twice.

Federal authorities began examining the disclosure in 2017. Prosecutor John Durham recommended against bringing criminal charges in December 2018, according to Comey's lawyers.

A second investigation, launched in 2019 under the code name "Tropical Vortex," was also closed without charges in February 2020.

How are Comey's lawyers fighting the new charges?

The Justice Department filed a legal document known as a "criminal information" in early October, shortly before the 10-year deadline for prosecuting the alleged offense.

Unlike an indictment, a criminal information does not require approval from a grand jury or judge.

Prosecutors say the filing allows them to extend the statute of limitations, which determines how long authorities have to bring criminal charges.

Comey's lawyers dispute that interpretation. They argue that federal law explicitly requires an indictment within 10 years and that the government's filing does not meet that requirement.

They have asked a judge to dismiss the case. A ruling is still pending.

Comey's attorney, Patrick Fitzgerald, also pointed to the two earlier investigations.

"Both times the Government determined that no charges should be brought against anyone," he said.

Responding to the latest allegations in a video posted on Substack, Comey condemned the prosecution.

"It would almost be funny if it weren't such an appalling abuse of the Department of Justice," he said.

"I'm still innocent. I'm still not afraid of these people, and I still believe in the independent federal judiciary."

What other criminal cases does James Comey face?

The latest case is the third criminal proceeding brought against Comey since Trump returned to the White House in January 2025.

In September 2025, prosecutors charged him with making false statements to Congress and obstructing a congressional proceeding.

A federal judge dismissed the case after finding that the Trump-appointed prosecutor who brought the charges had been unlawfully appointed.

In April 2026, Comey was indicted again, this time over an Instagram photograph showing seashells arranged to form the numbers "86 47."

The Justice Department interpreted the numbers as a threat against Trump, arguing that "86" referred to killing someone and "47" identified Trump as the 47th US president.

Comey denied threatening Trump's life and has sought to have that case dismissed.

Why has Trump targeted former FBI director Comey?

Comey was appointed FBI director in 2013 by Democratic President Barack Obama.

His relationship with Trump deteriorated shortly after the president took office in 2017.

Comey resisted Trump's request to pledge personal loyalty during a private dinner.

Trump fired him in May 2017 while the FBI was investigating Russian interference in the 2016 presidential election and possible connections to Trump's campaign.

The investigation was subsequently taken over by special counsel Robert Mueller. It established that Russia had interfered in the election but found insufficient evidence to prove criminal coordination between Moscow and Trump's campaign.

The two men have remained bitter political opponents. Trump has repeatedly accused Comey of treason, while Comey compared the president to a mafia boss in his 2018 memoir.

Edited by: Wesley Dockery

entries.title: England and Bayern Munich striker Harry Kane wins Ballon d'Or
entries.summary: The England captain ends his country's 25-year wait for the prestigious award after scoring 73 goals for club and country last season, beating competition from Lamine Yamal and Kylian Mbappe.
entries.content:
October 27, 2026

The England captain ends his country's 25-year wait for the prestigious award after scoring 73 goals for club and country last season, beating competition from Lamine Yamal and Kylian Mbappe.

England captain Harry Kane won the men's Ballon d'Or for the first time on Monday, becoming the first English player to receive the prestigious football award since 2001.

The 33-year-old Bayern Munich striker was honored at a ceremony at the London Palladium after scoring 73 goals in 65 appearances for club and country last season.

The Ballon d'Or, awarded by French magazine France Football, is one of football's most prestigious individual honors, recognizing the world's best players.

The last English player to win the award was former Liverpool striker Michael Owen, who claimed the prize 25 years ago.

Why did Harry Kane win the 2026 Ballon d'Or?

Kane's remarkable goalscoring record helped Bayern Munich secure a German league and cup double last season.

The former Tottenham Hotspur forward also led England to the World Cup semifinals, the country's best finish since winning the tournament in 1966.

Kane has finished as the Bundesliga's leading scorer for three consecutive seasons. He was also Europe's top club goalscorer during the 2025-26 campaign.

At Monday's ceremony, Kane thanked his Bayern Munich teammates for their support.

"Without you guys (his Bayern Munich team-mates) and the rest of the team it wouldn't be possible, the way you guys push me, the way we compete. So thank you very much," he said.

Kane also paid tribute to his former club Tottenham Hotspur, which he joined at the age of 11, as well as his England teammates and family.

"To my wife Kate, my best friend. We've been through ups and downs. You are my biggest support and I felt like you wanted this more than me," he said.

Reflecting on his career, Kane encouraged young footballers to pursue their ambitions despite setbacks.

"I hope my journey, it wasn't straightforward, I didn't go straight to the top, I had to experience a lot of loan moves and fight my way to get to where I am now. I hope that can give you inspiration."

Kane faced strong competition from Barcelona's Spanish teenager Lamine Yamal and Real Madrid's French forward Kylian Mbappe.

He joins Stanley Matthews, Bobby Charlton, Kevin Keegan and Owen among the English players to have won the award.

Who else won at the 2026 Ballon d'Or awards?

Spain midfielder Alexia Putellas claimed the women's Ballon d'Or for the third time in her career, having previously won the award in 2021 and 2022.

The 32-year-old was recognized after a successful season with Barcelona, winning the treble and scoring 21 goals across all competitions.

Putellas also played a key role in Barcelona's Champions League triumph, contributing seven goals and seven assists during the campaign.

She joined English club London City Lionesses in July after spending 14 years at Barcelona.

Her victory ended a run of three consecutive Ballon d'Or wins by fellow Spaniard Aitana Bonmatí.

Barcelona's Lamine Yamal won the Kopa Trophy for the best young male player for the third consecutive year, while his teammate Vicky Lopez claimed the women's award for the second year running.

Barcelona coach Pere Romeu was named women's coach of the year, while Spain manager Luis de la Fuente won the men's coaching award.

Spain goalkeeper Unai Simon received the men's Yashin Trophy, with Cata Coll winning the women's equivalent.

Barcelona was named women's club of the year, while Paris Saint-Germain took the men's award.

Edited by: Wesley Dockery
